subtopic: REPORT OF THE CLERK OF PETITIONS

speechtext:
On motions being called, the following report was presented:
The Clerk of Petitions has the honour to report that he has examined the following petition, viz.:
Of James Arthur Collins of Chisholm, province of Alberta, lumberman; praying that the House of Commons will investigate the conduct of the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada, the returning officer for the electoral district of Peace River, the deputy returning officer, and such other officer or officers as may be necessary, in connection with the establishing of a polling place at Brule Mines, poll No. 4 aforesaid and (the taking of, the counting and recounting the votes cast at such poll in the said district of Peace River, and that such Chief Electoral Officer, returning officer, deputy returning officer or other officer or officers be directed to take such action as may be requisite and necessary to secure the return to the House of Commons of the candidate who secured the greatest number of votes in the said electoral district of Peace River on the 29th of October, 1925, and finds that:
The prayer of this petition consists of two parts viz,-(1) That the House investigate the conduct of certain officials in connection with the election of a member to represent the constituency of Peace River in the House of Commons of Canada, held on the 29th October, 1925.
(2) That the House direct the proper officers to take such action as may be necessary and requisite to secure the return to the House of Commons of the candidate who secured the greatest number of votes cast by the electors of the said electoral district of Peace River on the 29th October, aforesaid.
The form of this petition and its contents so far as the first part of the prayer is concerned are within the requirements of the 75th rule, and refer only to such matters as are within the right and competency of the House to deal with, should the House desire to do so; should, however, the course suggested in the second part of the prayer be taken by the House it would apparently have the effect of authorizing other persons to - exercise a power which the House has already ^legated by statute to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts.
Apparently the first part of the prayer of this petition is only of a preliminary nature leading up to the main request as contained in the second part, consequently the prayer, considered as a whole, brings this petition within the ruling of Mr. Speaker Lemieux given on the 6th May last, in a somewhat similar case, which ruling was subsequently sustained by the House on appeal, viz, that a petition which prays for any action to be taken by tffe House that might involve in any respect an interference with the provisions of the Controverted Elections Act, chapter 7, R.S.C., 1906, cannot be received.
Under these circumstances I have therefore the honour to report that this petition should not be received.
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 154 to amend the Yukon Quartz Mining Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The object of this bill is simply to bring in line the provisions of the regulations which existed before the introduction of the bill in 1924. There was considerable doubt as to whether the act of 1924 had provided that all the agreements under the regulations with individuals who had staked claims should be carried out, and this is for the purpose of clarifying that matter. So far as the provisions of the bill are concerned, it is made retroactive to the date mentioned in the bill.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
I beg to move, in accordance with the notice given:
That on and after Monday, the 7th of June, 1926, until the end of the present session, the House shall meet at two o'clock in the afternoon of each sitting day.
Motion agreed to.

Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Prime Minister) moved:
That on Wednesday, the 2nd of June, 1926, and subsequent Wednesdays to the end of the session, the sittings of the House shall in every respect be under the same rules as provided foT other days.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to protest against this motion. I know of no other body of men in this country who have to work both night and day. We have been here for nearly five months; we have spent six weeks in I think useless debate on the Address, about five weeks more on the budget debate, to which only a few members listened and those who did listen did so simply that the House might have a quorum. Now at this late hour in the session, when we are doing business, we have just accepted a motion from the Prime Minister to sit an extra hour each day-I heartily approve of that-but I certainly think a protest should be made against this resolution to

Wednesday Evening Sittings
take the one night which we have in the week. I believe this House could do its business far better if we did without night sittings altogether. I see no reason why a body of sensible and reasonable men could not devise rules under which we would not need to sit both night and day.
I have read lately with much interest a speech which was delivered in this House in the year 1907. I would like to present to the House, and I will guarantee not to take more than a few minutes, a few of the statements made on that occasion by Mr. Wright, the then member for South Renfrew, because they deal with this particular question and they seem to me to be very pertinent.
Mr. Wright on that occasion called attention to the long hours that had to be put in and the arduous work that a private member had to do if he took his duties seriously, as I think everj'- member of parliament should. I know personally of one member of this House, who was at work yesterday morning at twenty minutes to nine. That member was still here last night at midnight, and was then asked to vote on a motion to adjourn the debate. Any member who voted against that motion was liable to the censure of a large number of the members of this House. That member had to be here again this morning to attend to his correspondence, then he had to attend a certain committee at 10.30, stay there until one o'clock, then rush out and get his lunch, and get back to this chamber at three o'clock this afternoon, and possibly he will be required to stay here until midnight again to-night. I ask the House and the government if that is a sensible way to carry on the business of this country. If these remarks apply to the private member, they apply with even greater force to the Prime Minister and to the members of the government. What chance have these men to get a decent night's sleep under such conditions? What chance has the leader of the opposition? The leader of the opposition, as we all know, to our regret, has been confined to his home through illness recently, and I have no doubt that it was largely brought on by the arduous duties he is called upon to perform and the long hours he is compelled to spend in this House.
I would also draw the attention of members of the House to the fact that we have here in this chamber a large number of pages, most of whom I understand are orphans, or boys without fathers. They come here because it is necessary for them to earn a living. In most of the provinces in Canada we have an act to prevent children being employed after certain hours at night in factories, but in this

"factory of words and phrases," as Mr. Wright describes it, these poor boys are compelled sometimes to stay all night-on Wednesday night as well as other nights if this motion carries.
I have no hope, Mr. Speaker, of preventing this resolution carrying and of preventing this House from being compelled to sit on Wednesday night, but I think a protest should be made on every possible occasion against the procedure which compels members to stay here both night and day.
What I propose is this: Let us meet, say. at one o'clock in the afternoon and sit till six. If we did that, with proper rules, we should get through the business of this House in four months. As Mr. Wright pointed out in his speech in 1907, almost every parliament in the world, with the exception of those of Great Britain and Canada, carries on its 'business without night sessions at all. I think it is high time that private members on all sides of this House should exercise a little bit of their power and demand of all parties in the House that some reform of the rules shall be made so that we shall not be compelled to sit here four, and now five, nights in the week to most unearthly hours. Mr. Wright said on that occasion that we were citizens of a Christian country and were supposed to do our work in daylight and sleep at night. I think I cannot do better than simply impress that idea upon the House before I sit down. I think that all parties are equally guilty of allowing the business of this House to drift until we get into this position, where it seems necesary to sit every night in the week, and before the end of the session, no doubt, we shall sometimes have to sit all night.	*
Move an amendment.

I do not think I should move an amendment. The leader of the opposition said a week ago that he was quite willing to sit on Wednesday night, and I think possibly the House wishes to sit on Wednesday night so as to get through, but I do want to emphasize this: If we had adopted suitable amendments to the rules early this session, or at the last session, we would not now be required to sit five nights a week.
Motion agreed to.

If the examiner has the right to go into the substance and purpose, and to say to parliament whether or not it shall receive a petition, we have come to a very fine pass in responsible and democratic government. I submit to you that the form alone comes within his disposition; that if it is within his functions to dictate to this House now that we must not even receive the petition of Collins, then it must have been his opinion on the first presentation of the petition that we should not receive it and apparently his opinion at that time differed from that of Your Honour. I therefore will ask you now, or if this occasion is not fitting, on a suitable occasion, to rule that this report from the examiner is entirely beyond his power and to instruct him to report within his powers and duties.

subtopic: BILL AUTHORIZING TRANSFER TO ALBERTA

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL AUTHORIZING TRANSFER TO ALBERTA
speechtext:
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated yesterday, in answer to a question by the right hon. leader of the opposition, that I would make a statement to-day concerning legislation with regard to the natural resources of Alberta, and I will now do so:
By the agreement entered into on the 9th day of January, 1926, between the government of the Dominion and the government of Alberta, all crown lands within the province are to be transferred to the province, subject to any trust existing in respect thereof.
In 1872, after the acquisition by the Dominion government of the Northwest Territories, the first statute concerning Dominion public lands was enacted. It is chapter 23 of 35 Victoria. Section 22 of this act created an education endowment, sections 11 and 29 in every surveyed township to be set apart for purposes of education, in the territory.
In 1879, statute 42 Victoria, chapter 31, placed under the Minister of the Interior the administration of the school lands and the school fund derived from the sale of such lands, the interest thereon to be paid annually to the government of the province or territory within which such lands are situated, for school purposes. Those statutes have been consolidated from time to time, namely: in 1908, 1914, 1916, 1919, 1920, 1921, 1923, 1924. The administration of those school lands and the school fund by the Dominion government has always been considered as a trust and, to use the language of Sir John A. Macdonald, in 1883, page 874 of the Debates : " The Dominion government is merely 
the trustee for these lands and cannot divert them in any way whatever from the purpose of school endowment
It thus appeared to the government that it was advisable to make it clear that the transfer of the school lands and the school lands fund should be made subject to that trust, and that they should continue to be administered by the province in accordance with the existing laws under the constitution of Alberta.
I am responsible for the drafting of the clause which is in the resolution on the order paper, the object of which was to continue the existing order of things.
Colonel Biggar, who is counsel for the government of Canada, and who had been entrusted with the legal work concerning the agreement with Alberta, went to Edmonton to submit this new clause, and said clause was accepted by the government of Alberta and by the law officers of the province.
The clause, as drafted, was inserted in the bill introduced by the Alberta government in the legislature of that province on February 24, and the bill received its second reading, on March 5 passed through the committee stage, and stood for third reading.
Simultaneously, the clause was inserted in the legislation introduced by the Dominion government and is part of the resolution on the order paper concerning said legislation.
Two other amendments concerning the parks, forest reserves and the rights and properties of the Hudson's Bay Company were also suggested by us, accepted by Alberta, and inserted in the concurrent legislation at the same time.
On April 7th the Premier of Alberta sent a telegram that owing to an editorial in a certain newspaper he would probably have to recommit the bill and amend it.
The criticism of the newspaper in question was to the effect that the clause as drafted would result in the Imperial parliament giving ratification to the school clause of the Alberta Act of 1905, which according to the writer of the editorial, was unconstitutional.
Our answer was that any attempt to change the clause under such circumstances, would be resented, and could not be accepted.
The telegram of Mr. Brownlee, on April 7, was the first intimation to me that there could be any doubt as to the validity or the constitutionality of section 17 of the Alberta Act. The clause which I suggested never was drafted for the purpose of giving to section 17 the ratification which an imperial act would involve. Indeed it is my opinion-as it was the opinion of those who placed that section in the constitution of Alberta-that

Alberta Natural Resources
the act of 1905 has the effect of an imperial enactment for all purposes and that its validity is beyond question.
Section 17 of the Alberta Act is the result of a compromise and was placed in the constitution to prevent litigation and for the purpose of continuing in Alberta the system existing in 1905. This compromise was accepted to settle and put an end to a difficult problem.
On May 25, a telegram was received by the Prime Minister from Premier Brownlee, informing him that the provincial legislature had passed the Natural Resources Bill with an amendment to clause 2 (a), substituting for the last words of said clause the following:
For the support of schools organized and carried on therein in accordance with the law of the province.
The amendment made by the legislature of Alberta without our consent suggests that the laws of the province might differ from or be in conflict with section 17 of the Constitutional Act of Alberta. Otherwise the amendment would be useless and futile. Furthermore, the record, as well as the statements made, show that the change is made owing to the expression of a doubt in some quarters as to the validity of the Alberta Act. This is unacceptable to us.
The Alberta Act has stood as the constitution of the province for twenty-one years. It has come directly and indirectly before all the courts of the land without its constitutionality being challenged or doubted, except in one instance before the courts of Alberta, where its validity was upheld. We cannot directly or indirectly, even in a tacit manner, acknowledge that its validity might be subject to question.
However the Prime Minister has stated to Mr. Brownlee that if the government of Alberta is willing to question the validity of the act, we will gladly facilitate and expedite proceedings, so that a reference to the courts may take place immediately.
In justice to Mr. Brownlee, I must say that he does not personally question the validity of the Alberta Act. His suggestion seems rather to be that as there are some people who have doubts about it, we should refrain from any reference to it in our legislation.
Our present position in the matter is fairly expressed in a telegram sent to the Premier of Alberta on May 27 by the Prime Minister. This telegram, after reciting the history of the negotiations, continues as follows:
As pointed out in interview at Ottawa, an view of implied doubts as to the validity of Constitution Act any amendment to the Natural Resources Bill as originally agreed upon if introduced at this stage of the proceedings and having reference directly or indirectly to school lands would be certain to raise controversy over school question. In these circumstances we do not feel that we would be justified in submitting to our parliament the amendment made by the Alberta legislature on Saturday Hast, and quoted in your wire. This amendment as adopted by your house if it has any meaning suggests that the laws of the province might differ from or be in conflict with the Alberta Act. Sureily the laws of the province must be within the four corners of the constitution which is the source of her legislative powers. Clearly the whole matter hinges on the validity of Alberta Act which you stated some people were questioning. We agree with you that every available means Should be taken to avoid a possible controversy on the school question. We believe further that question should be cleared away and settled for all time. We have offered to facilitate proceedings for a reference to the courts of the Alberta Act. We reiterate this offer and dn order to prevent delay, as well as to avoid any question being raised as to party who should be expected to initiate proceedings our government will take immediate steps for a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. We will submit the act and support and uphold its validity, and give an opportunity to those who question it to present their views. When question definitely settled, all difficulties as to the drafting of proposed legislation will disappear and negotiations with respect to transfer of resources may then be resumed in a manner which will remove altogether the possibility of the introduction of any school question.
This was signed by the Prime Minister. I may say that the Department of Justice has in hand the proceedings necessary for the submission of this question to the Supreme Court of Canada. I believe this solution is fair to all parties, and I earnestly hope that this delicate question will in this way be settled definitely and removed forever from the field of controversy.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF POST OFFICE INSPECTOR-MARITIME PROVINCES
speechtext:
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) asked a question yesterday with reference to the appointment of a post office inspector in the Maritime provinces. On behalf of the Postmaster General I desire to make this statement:
There are two postal districts in the Maritime provinces-one with headquarters at St. John and one at Halifax, also a post office inspector stationed at Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island.
To provide for inspection work in ithose portions of the province of New Brunswick with French speaking population, it was ifound necessary to have a bilingual inspector. It was considered that the bilingual inspector should be able to do all the bilingual work in the three Maritime provinces. He is, therefore, being stationed at Moncton in order to be more readily available for the three provinces although he is attached to the staff of the St. John postal district.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 148, for the purpose of establishing in Canada a system of Long Term Mortgage Credit for Farmers.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Duff in the chair.
Short title agreed to.
On section 2-Definitions.

Paragraph (d) defines a farmer to be any person whose business is 'solely" that of farming and who owns and occupies a farm, or who proposes to acquire a farm for immediate occupation and cultivation. A similar definition in the Bankruptcy	Act was interpreted by	Mr. Justice Tweedy in such a way as to exclude persons	engaged in	custom threshing.	Mr. Justice	Tweedy held that	the4 p.m. word "solely" restricted the provisions	of the Bankruptcy	Act
to those who were engaged strictly in farming, and he gave it as his opinion that men engaged in threshing along with farming were precluded from that act. If the word "solely" is retained in this 'bill the same difficulty will arise here, and the bill will be interpreted as excluding those farmers who also do custom threshing.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This qualifying word is intended to make it clear that anyone living in the village and occupied industrially is not to be considered a farmer within the meaning of the act merely because he happens to do some farming. It is not the intention to preclude any farmer from exercising his ordinary duties as a citizen. For instance, a member of parliament whose business, apart from his parliamentary duties, is farming is not excluded. The word has been inserted for the protection of the farmers themselves.

I would not raise the point were it not for the inter-

Long Term Farm Loans
pretation which Mr. Justice Tweedy placed on a similar definition in the Bankruptcy Act, whereby he excluded from the benefits of that legislation such farmers as I have described. I have no desire to widen the scope of the bill to embrace business men in towns, living away from their farms, and I may point out to the minister that such persons come under another section. I would move-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will move the amendment later.
The word "farmer" here means only the farmer of the soil. Why not make provision for the farmer of the sea, the fisherman? Why should he not be entitled to the provisions of this act?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend can explain to me how I can get a mortgage on the fish in the sea I will consider his suggestion.
You can get a mortgage on the fisherman's equipment as well as on the farmer's.

I support the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Short). The fishermen at least on the Atlantic coast, engage in an occupation which at times is quite precarious, and they are entitled to some encouragement at the hands of this parliament while we are considei'ing the needs of the farmers of the west. I seriously suggest that if the minister has not already done so he should include fishermen in the benefits of the act. There is no difficulty about security. The equipment of the fishermen is as saleable in their districts as is the security of the farmer in Alberta, especially in the drought season. If anything, the advantage in this respect is with the fisherman. If there is to be any easy money for a particular class, then let us have no discrimination in favour of the western farmer. I am willing that he should receive fair treatment, but I do not want to see him get any special privileges. And that is all this legislation amounts to. I am not by any means opposed to rural credits, but if the government, desire to put easy and cheap money in the way of the farmers of the west, I demand at least equal treatment on behalf of the fishermen of the Maritime provinces.
This is the first time the suggestion has been made that this legislation is for the benefit of the west alone; I thought it was intended to benefit all Canada.

Everyone knows that for
the past five years hon. members to my left have been demanding legislation of this character for the particular benefit of their own 14011-249
constituents. There has never been a demand from the farmers of the Maritime provinces for legislation of this kind.
Then they are not properly represented.

They were not properly
represented in the last parliament but the3' are well represented in this House. Speaking for the Maritime provinces, our farmers do not and will not demand this kind of help if you will give us a proper fiscal policy.

I would like the minister
to explain the definitions under clause 2, because I am very doubtful whether parliament has power to pass this bill. Why should there be rural credits and not city credits; why single out the farmers for long term loans? Why should this particular class be favoured as against all others? Agriculture to-day is the most highly protected industry in the world, and this is class legislation of the worst kind; one class is favoured because they have an influence in this House which other classes do not have.

I rise to a point of order.
I contend that the hon. gentleman is not speaking to the section of this bill under discussion.
In the first place, Mr. Chairman-

I ask for a ruling on the
point of order, Mr. Chairman.
I say this is class legislation of the worst kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I rise more particularly to
move the amendment which I have just handed you, Mr. Chairman, that the word "solely" be deleted. The discussion we have had so far only emphasizes the difficulties of legislating for a large country of varied interests such as Canada. This is the first time it has been brought to my attention that the fishermen require legislation of this kind. This government has not been unmindful of the fishermen; in the budget of 1924 we made considerable concessions to those engaged in this industry, making it easier for them to get their equipment and so earn a living.
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When I get through I will
answer my hon. friend. This measure is designed to help not only the farmers of the prairie provinces but those of the entire Dominion. The necessity for such a measure to provide cheaper money for the man on the farm has been demonstrated to us time after

Long Term Farm Loans

time. The man on the land produces traffic for the railways and his success determines the general prosperity of the country. This government has even been accused of being a bit tardy in introducing this legislation. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) had a similar resolution on the order paper the day parliament opened, and I give him credit for being in favour of this move. Most of the provinces have systems of rural credits of one kind or another; they have already recognized the necessity for such a measure as we are bringing in now, The hon. members for Ontario may object to this, because in Ontario they have a very excellent system of rural credits which, I am told, is on a good paying basis.
Why duplicate it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are not duplicating it;
it is not necessary for Ontario to come under this scheme if they do not want to, but because Ontario is well provided for is no reason why the other provinces should not be helped. It is not obligatory upon any province to come under this scheme if they do not wish to. Now coming back to the fishermen, I will be very pleased to listen to my hon. friends who represent these people if they can establish the necessity for a system of credits other than those now provided by the rural credit systems of the provinces. We will consider that question at another session, but this act has to do with long term mortgage credits for farmers. I move the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Robb moves that
subsection (d) of section 2 be amended by deleting the word "solely" in the first line.

I have no objection whatever to this bill, but why confine it to soil farmers? The fisherman farms the sea just as much as the soil farmer farms the land, and he has just as hard a time to make a living as the farmer on the land. Consequently he is entitled to just as much consideration. Before the fisherman can start out to make a living he has to spend from $500 to $1,000 on equipment; many men are not in a position to make such an expenditure, and they must be assisted. If the land farmer is to be helped with easy money I claim that the fishermen of the Martime provinces and the Pacific coast should be helped as well. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) would be well advised to take this into consideration before the measure passes.

I think it would be well for the minister to consider our fishermen. As has been pointed out, they are put to a
IMr. Robb.]
considerable expense in connection with their equipment, nets, motor boats and so on, and at this particular time the fishermen along the Northumberland straits are having a very difficult time to raise sufficient money to equip themselves properly. Within the last two or three years, because of poor facilities, they have had some considerable difficulty in protecting their boats from storms along the cap Bald coast. This is particularly true in connection with the French Acadian people. They have had a hard time; their expenses have been high; they have sustained considerable losses, and if something is to be done to assist them it should be done at this time. The western farmers have been given every, assistance; they have had opportunities not afforded to other classes. The farmers and fishermen in the Maritime provinces are paying rates to-day 100 per cent higher than those paid by the farmers in the west for the same haul.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order.
Mr. Chairman. I submit that if we are to have a new budget debate, if we are going to debate freight rates at this time, we will be here all summer. If my hon. friend will confine himself to the question at issue we will get along more quickly, and he can discuss freight rates at another time.

I am merely pointing out
that the fishermen are entitled to just as much consideration as are the farmers in western Canadia, and it is on their behalf that I am speaking, in order that they may be given opportunities to share in the same benefits which this government is bestowing on the farmers of the west. I think the fishermen deserve every consideration. They go through more hardships than the farmer; they work harder and take more chances, and their occupation is more hazardous. I think if some of the members of this House who have not seen the fishing industry being carried on would take a trip down to the Maritime provinces and see what these men have to go through, the chances they have to take and the storms they have to fight in their boats, they would agree with me that these men are deserving of more consideration than they have received in the past. Personally I am opposed to anything being done under this bill unless the fishermen along the Atlantic coast are also taken into consideration.

I feel reasonably sure
that there is not a single member of this committee who would not agree that the fisherman is equally entitled to consideration from this House with the farmer or anyone

Long Term Farm Loans
else, but may I point out with.regard to the measure now before us, that it deals with a particular type of credit as relating even to the farming industry, that particular type of credit being long term mortgage credit based upon the security of land. It does not deal with short term credit based on the security of chattels either on the farm or anywhere else. I listened to my hon. friends from the Maritime provinces, and if I understand the requirements of the fishing industry correctly from what they tell me, it is rather short term credit on chattel security that is required for that industry. Manifestly it is not possible for the fisherman to give a mortgage on the sea, and it would not be any good if he did so. He has certain equipment that he uses in his business-

What about his fishing
stand? That is real property.
Does he have real property? I would like to get to know.
He has his home as well.

I listened to what my hon. friends had to say, and they spoke of fishing gear and the expense the fisherman was put to in order to equip himself to carry on his business. Everything that was mentioned by my hon. friends was in the nature of a chattel, and I therefore came to the conclusion, perhaps erroneously, but at least based upon the info-mation supplied by my hon. friends, that the type of security available in connection with that industry is analogous to What the farmer has to give with respect to his short term credit requirements, and therefore does not and cannot very well come within the scope of this bill. Personally I would like to learn more about the fishing industry, and if there is 'any way to assist any one of our primary industries by way of facilitating credit, not at the expense of the country, but with the backing of the country, I can assure my hon. friends from the Maritime provinces that it will have my support.

I was on my feeit when the
minister rose, to express exactly the same opinions he has expressed. I want to say on behalf of the farmers in the west that we have every sympathy with the fishermen and their troubles. In my young days I lived close by the sea, and know something of the hardships of the fishermen. I remember one storm in which 138 fishermen found a watery grave in one afternoon. So no one needs to tell me about the hardships of the fishermen on the sea. But I want to point out that this bill is 14011-249J
not applicable to the circumstances in which the fishermen find themselves. We in this part of the House have been working for four years to get such a bill as we have now before us, and this is the first time we have heard anything in connection with helping the fishermen in this way. If our friends from the Maritime provinces will come back next session with some workable bill to provide not easy money, but cheap money-there is a difference-to help the fishermen in their calling, or any other primary industry in this Dominion, I am sure they will find us heartily with them.
We are very glad to get the information from the deputy Prime M nister that the fishermen of the Maritime provin.es rill receive consideration at the next session.

There are a large numbe
of farmers in Gaspe and Bonaventure who ar at the same time fishermen; they carry on both callings. When fishing is not over plentiful, they resort more extensively t' farming, and I would like to have that class included, if possible, under this bill. A mm who can give security on land, whether he i.-a fisherman or not, should not be debarred from the benefits of this legislation.

I endorse the suggestion
of the hon. member for Bonaventure. It i-true that a large number of the fishermen in the Maritime provinces also carry on farming and they nearly all own real property of some sort.

Then they are already
under this bill.

I am not so sure that they are. I would point out for the benefit of the hon. member for Brandon, if he has not heard a specific demand made on behalf of the fishermen, that this is the first concrete proposal of this kind that has been made in five years. This is the first occasion on which a concrete demand of this kind could be made on behalf of the fishermen, and that is why it is being made. So far as his invitation to wait for another year is concerned. I think we ought to decline that invitation with thanks. Now is the accepted time. If we are going to do anything for the fishermen in the Maritime provinces, we want to do it now. Therefore I invite the minister to amend the bill in that regard, so that it will take in any fisherman who is able to give security other than chattel security, and he might also take into consideration, if he will, the question of chattel security. I quite appreciate the difficulty of including short term

Long Term Farm Loans
credits in a bill of this character, as it is not designed for that, and therefore I shall not press that point; but I do press upon the minister the desirability of assisting these fishermen and bringing them within the terms of this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I gather from the observations of my friend from York-Sunbury and my hon. friend from Bonaventure that the amendment I have just introduced brings in most of the fishermen of the Maritime provinces. The word " solely " is stricken out, so that the farmer who has land would come in under this act anyway. I think my hon. friend should leave it to a pretty generous interpretation by the board.
Would a fisherman's occupation be farming? That is what the definition says.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If, as the hon. member for Bonaventure and the hon. member for York-Sunbury have said, these men are farmers as well as fishermen, they certainly would not be deprived of their privileges as farmers simply because they were incidentally engaged in fishing.

The minister knows
quite well that the men referred to by the hon. members are fishermen. The farm they have is incidental to their calling of fishing, and while it might perhaps be security for something, farming is not their main occupation, and they would never come in under this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my right hon. friend, who is a pretty good economist, has any amendment to suggest-

I have not suggested
anything of the sort, but I do not want the minister to cast aside an amendment on a mere sophism which has nothing in it.

If the minister will refer to paragraph (b) of section 4, he will see that it gives the board power:
To make 'long term loans to farmers on the security of first mortgages on farm lands.
Suppose the fisherman has his little homestead of a few acres. It has a commercial value in the community, and it may be good security for a loan, but I doubt whether under this section the board would have power to make him a loan. More than that, as pointed out by the leader of the opposition, his main business must be farming. That man will not benefit by this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I read carefully the resolution put on the order paper by the hon. member
J
for Vancouver, and I listened to the speech delivered by my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, and I concluded that when this bill was introduced it would meet at least with their approval, as it contained what they had outlined as necessary for farming. I ask the hon. member for York-Sunbury if he has read this bill all through. He is a good lawyer, a good financier; does he think we can go out and sell bonds on security such as he has just mentioned?

I think probably you will
sell bonds on much poorer security than you will in the case of some of the farm loans that will be mad& under this legislation, especially in the province of New Brunswick to-day. Does the minister know how difficult it is under the conditions existing down there for farmers to obtain loans now in the open market-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This will make it easier for
them.
-due to the fiscal policy of this government driving industry out of our towns and cities?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is another question.

It may be, but that condition is due to the policy of this government. I am not in a position to submit an amendment. However, I should be glad to consult with the minister on the point. I am really serious albout the matter. I think something can be done, and if ever anything is to be done now is the accepted time.

I notice a very general
impression in the House-at any rate the view seems to be held by many of the members-that no reference has been made previously to the desirability of extending to the fisherman treatment similar to that granted to the farmer. That is not quite correct. At least once before, and I think probably on two occasions, I have heard the suggestion made that fishermen should be included in this bill.
So have I.

Therefore it is not the
first time the point has been raised. On the contrary, I think the records will show that on several occasions in the past the claims of the fishermen have been put forward. Now, most fishermen possess more than mere chattels. Most of them own their houses, and many of them a few acres of land. I think the minister will need to consider very carefully the definition of what constitutes a farmer. I fear many difficulties will arise

Long Term Farm Loans
and there will be douibt in some cases as to whether the applicant can be considered a farmer or not. Take the case of a fisherman who earns his living substantially by fishing, who also has an acre or two on which he and his family carry on kitchen gardening, would he be regarded as a farmer under the proposed legislation? The minister says "no". Then there will need to be a little better definition in order to determine what will constitute a farmer in the case of a man who is also engaged in fishing.
Do I understand there will be no doubt in the minister's mind that farmers who are also fruit growers will come within the purview of this definition?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely.

That being so, I desire to
concur in what has been said by the speakers who have just preceded me with regard to the farmer. In this connection may I thank the minister for his promise to take the matter into consideration next year, also the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) for his promise to give consideration to the case of the fishermen of 'the Maritime provinces. What I object to, and what our people also object to, is that when it comes to doing something for the Maritime provinces we are told "We will ibe glad to do it to-morrow or next year." But when it is a case of doing something for other parts of the country we are told "We insist on its being done now." I think that attitude will meet with very considerable criticism, particularly on the part of the people of the Maritime provinces.
I noticed another statement which struck me as rather peculiar. It was that no mention of the rights of the fishermen had been made in this House in the last four years. I thought that was an amazing statement in view of the fact that we had a solid delegation in this House representing the province of Nova Scotia at least. We sometimes hear the statement that the fishermen are prosperous and that the industry has been greatly extended as a result of wider markets. Let me point out that in 1919 the province of Nova Scotia produced $15,171,929 worth of fish. In 1922, the first year that this government had an opportunity to develop wider markets, the production dropped to $10,209,2.58, In 1923 there was a further drop of $1,800,000 down to $8,448,385. In 1924 the drop still continued to $8,277,000, and in 1925 the production was still going down. And yet we heard statements in this House during the budget debate that the fishing industry of Nova Scotia had been flourishing under the
policy of the government for the last four years. But we have the concrete fact before us that in five years the fishing industry has declined to the extent of $7,000,000. Nevertheless when there is an opportunity to do something to increase the fish production of Nova Scotia, as well as that of the other Maritime provinces, we are told by the leader of the Progressive party:	"Oh, come back
next year and we will give you something." The minister also says, "Make your suggestions and demands during the next year and we will consider them. This legislation is for the farmer alone, and only those farmers in the provinces where they desire to avail themselves of it." I submit that when we are considering this legislation, even if it takes another twenty-four hours to frame an effective amendment, we should take such action as will ensure that the various other industries in the country shall also benefit by the impetus we desire to give the farming industry.

I quite realize that under the proposed legislation it is impracticable to grant relief to all the fishermen, as has been stated by some hon. gentlemen opposite. However, I take the position very strongly that if there is any industry that should receive consideration from the government it is the fishing industry, not only of the Maritime provinces but of Canada as a whole. I think that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House have endeavoured to present the views of the fishermen as strongly as they possibly could. Not only have propositions been brought before the select standing committee on Marine and Fisheries, but wre have been asking for concrete action by this House so as to give some assistance to the fishing industry in the Maritime provinces. The question has been raised as to -who will receive benefit under this system of loans and what really constitutes a farmer-whether a fisherman farmer or a farmer fisherman can be properly included in that category'-. I judge that the individual who has sufficient land free from encumbrance to give the requisite security can receive benefits under this act?
Why does the hon. member say that? I fear he has not read the bill.

I do not see anything in the bill that will deprive any man who has sufficient land free from encumbrance to give the needed security from receiving the benefits contemplated. It cannot be argued that because a man engages in fishing as well as farming he shall be excluded
Long Term Farm Loans

from the proposed benefits. It will be just as reasonable to argue that a farmer in the Northwest Territories should not be granted assistance under this legislation because he worked at lumbering, or some other calling, for a few months in the year. I think any man in any part of the Dominion with sufficient real estate in his own name will receive the benefits under the act. If not, I am not correctly informed on this matter. However I wish to place myself on record as making a demand on behalf of the fishing industry of the Maritime provinces. We were asking for concessions in the putting up of a certain preparation made from the lobster, which is being wasted at present, but which would have meant an immense revenue to the lobster packers and fishermen of the Maritime provinces. We could not get that small concession, because other larger interests and the larger packer's wished to control the situation, and, as in all such cases, the small man had to go without his concession. I wish to support anything that will tend to benefit the fishing industry, and I am sure that the Marine and Fisheries estimates will afford opporunity for further discussion of this matter. I think we should concentrate our efforts on those estimates and endeavour to obtain some assistance.

I am not rising to say anything against loans to fishermen, but I would not like any hon. member to go home with the false hope in his mind that there is going to be any loan to fishermen under this act. It is especially forbidden by the act. It does not matter how much land he owns; he might own the whole of Prince Edward Island, but if his occupation is that of fisherman he cannot get anything."
A man may have two occupations-farmer and fisherman.

A man has an occupation which is his chief occupation always, and you could not select anyone in the whole of the island whose occupation you could not tell. A man is one or the other. It may be he has a few onions or patches of corn, but he is a fisherman. He cannot get anything under this measure. Whether he should or not is not the question we are discussing. He could not get anything, and we might as well cease trying to delude the fishermen, or those who do not read, into thinking that they could get anything. For my part I am in favour of the rural credits measure. I stated so when the matter was discussed on a previous occasion, and I hope this measure will be along lines to meet my desire in respect to such a measure. I do not know that you could, in

the first instance, include other industries in it, but you could accompany this measure by another along similar lines, or different lines, to achieve the same end for that other class of people. But the rural credit measure is simply a measure to provide for rural credits, and I think it is time we set. our minds to work to frame a measure satisfactory to the rural sections of the country. We are not at the stage where the vital provisions should be discussed, but we are at the definitions;. I listened to the point raised by my hon. friend from Bow River, which I think the minister conceded, but I really do not think it is of so much consequence as another point, although I fancy it is right. Under this definition, in order to get a loan, a man must be residing on and occupying the land. If the minister will read his definition carefully he will see the point I am trying to make. Paragraph (d) of clause 2 reads:
"Farmer" means any person whose business is that of farming.
The word "solely" is now struck out. The paragragh continues:
And who owns and occupies a farm, or who proposes to acquire a farm for immediate occupation and cultivation by him.
The question I put to the minister is this: does he have to occupy that farm the year round, save of course a trip to California, or to parliament, or anything of that sort, where he does not take up another residence? What I have in mind is a large class of farmers who occupy their farms only for the summer, and reside in a village or town almost half the year. Under this clause as it now reads that man could not obtain a loan.

He really would need the
loan more than the man who remained on his farm all the time.

Yes, especially if he
went to California. This would not be the farm he occupies the year round, as his only place of abode. There are very many farmers who do not, in the sense of this definition, occupy a farm at all. They do not live on it. I know some of the best farmers in Manitoba who live in the town or village the year round, but who thoroughly cultivate their farms. They are excluded by this definition from getting a loan. If the minister intends that that should be the position, that is another question, but I do not think that he does. The next point is that it should not be enough that a man owns and occupies a farm. I might occupy a farm near a little town and do nothing

Long Term Farm Loans
with it. The man should own and cultivate the farm. The word "cultivate" should be substituted for the w'ord "occupy." If a man owns and cultivates a farm, I would not care where he lived. It should be sufficient that he is cultivating the farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend will
proceed he would notice that in the very clause he is quoting cultivation is provided for.

No, that is only in the
case of the man who has no farm at all, but is going to get one. Where the draughtsman made the slip was this: he provided in the case of a man who did not have a farm, and was going to get one, that he should get the loan because he was going to get the farm and cultivate it. If he already owned it he would not need to cultivate it. All he needed to do was to occupy it.

I think the act would
cover that point.

Does not the word "occupy" as it is used here really mean " cultivate "? A man may have a business located on a business street, and may occupy a house in a different part of the town. It could be said that he occupied the store he owned. It seems to me that is the interpretation that should be given to the clause.

The point I referred to
a moment ago about the word "occupy" is perhaps covered, but the other point is not. If we insist on a man owning and cultivating land I do not see any sense of insisting on his living on it the whole or part of the year. He may live on the next farm. He may own a farm across the road and want a loan on it, and might cultivate it, but could not get the loan.
Under the interpretation the rigihit hon. gentleman places on the word " occupy " it is impossible for a man, although he was actually farming his land, but living in town, to get a loan.

No. I insist on his
cultivating it. The point I am making is that a man should not be compelled to occupy a farm on which he wants to get a loan.

Is not the clause capable
of a wider definition?
; I do not know of any other. Certainly if I live in town, have a farm six miles out, and cultivate the farm I should be entitled to the loan.

The point is of very
great importance, but for a reason the opposite to that under discussion, that reason
being that it is not the intention of the act to provide loans for men who are incidentally farmers, that is men who are engaged in some other line of business. For instance, my right hon. friend is a farmer and I am a farmer, but not in the sense under which we wish to have credit extended under this law.
Speak for yourself.

I am speaking for
myself. I was very nearly putting my right hon. friend in the same category because I think he said on one occasion he did own a farm.
What I mean is: Do not exclude me from the benefits of this measure too soon.

I am excluding both my self and my right hon. friend. I still own my original farm; but from the point of view of public policy I do not think it is desirable that this law should be so wide that its facilities might be extended to a man such as myself who, although still farming a farm in the sense of being in control of its operations, meeting the bills and so forth, is not in the class of an actual resident, occupier farmer. There is another class of cases, the class who are engaged in some business in the near-by village. There is hardly a business man in a western village who is not also a farmer. I think all will agree that it is not desirable that we should extend the privileges of this legislation to that class of farmer who is farming as a side issue to some other business which is of much more importance in his scheme of things.
The minister has missed my point.	[DOT]

I know that is not my right hon. friend's point; but if the legislation is widened sufficiently to include the class of farmer to whom my right hon. friend refers, I am very much afraid that it will let in this other class. My right hon. friend has referred to the man who lives in a village, who, unless quite incidentally, has no other occupation than farming, and who farms a farm three or four miles out of that village. As he has stated, there is a large and growing class of that type of farmer; but just how to cover the point and admit that class of farmer without also admitting the very much wider class of business men who farm incidentally is a difficulty which I have not been able to overcome.

That is all covered by
the definition of the farmer. Farming must
Long Term Farm Loans

be his business. Farming is certainly not the business of the minister and it is not mine. Once you have said that you have excluded all in the class to which the minister refers.

No. My right hon.
friend will permit me, he will know as I know of men who farm in a very large way and who also have some other business. It would be very difficult to determine which of those two was the main business. I have in mind men who farm as much as two or three thousand acres and who also live and are engaged in business in a town. In all probability the turn-over of the farm might very well be larger than the turn-over of the business in the town. The difficulty of determining which was the main business of the man concerned would be very great and I speak from some experience in that regard. If we widen the definition this will be a matter of great difficulty. As regards practical administration, regulations of the board can, I believe, deal with the type of case to which my right hon. friend refers if we give them just that much latitude. I say what I am saying merely as an argument against widening that latitude too much and the tendency is rather to widen it too much.

If the commission finds that the main business of any man is farming that man should come in just the same as anybody else. The object of this legislation is or should be to constitute a low interest, underlying financial security on loans. It will do just as much good to the community to grant a loan on land farmed by a man living in Portage la Prairie although the land is three miles out as to grant it to a man actually living on his farm. The object of it indeed is to encourage the cultivation of land and the production of goods therefrom by constituting a cheap underlying security and it should extend to all whose main business is farming. It does so extend under the definition, but you have a most unreasonable exclusion when you say that a man must be all the time living on his land. As the years go on you are going to exclude more and more until you have half the population of western Canada excluded from the legislation. There is no line of demarcation; there is no reason, no sense in it. The minister should either have it in that way or give the benefit to nobody.

I would
find myself largely in accord with the leader of the opposition if we could safeguard the loans made under this bill with regard to cases of this kind. You have in town a real estate agent or an implement agent who is

also a farmer. He applies for a loan under this bill; he secures the loan on the basis of the security of his farm; but without the consent or knowledge of the board he invests part of that loan in his real estate business or implement agency. Before the board discovers what has happened to the loan and is in a position to collect on the good security the man has failed. The board comes along and all it can do it to pick up the fragments. It has the man's security which may still be good; but wo do not want the scheme burdened with a great deal of real estate dealer's or implement agent's land which is being farmed by proxy. If that could be covered I would agree with the leader of the opposition.

The government must
follow the loan past the hands of the borrower; they must see that the money is properly applied. Surely they will not hand it over to the borrower and just let him do what he likes with it.
I hope not.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Having read carefully the reports made by Doctor Tory who was appointed to investigate this question, and having listened to the arguments of those who advance such a measure as this, my understanding is that we should provide not so much for a cheap method of financing loans as for a cheap method of helping the man who is really farming, the man who is on the land, to farm. That is where I differ somewhat from my right hon. friend. I would not want to widen this too much; I would like the measure to go through so that it would be regarded as a sound financial means of enabling the real farmer who is farming to get money at a reasonable price. The closer we can keep to that, the better value we put on those bonds when we come to sell them on the market.
After all, the man who invests money looks carefully into the matter to see whether it is a real farmer who is working the land or some chap who is carying the land along in the hope that some day it will increase in value and he will sell it. Having made this statement, I may say that my friend and colleague the Minister of Railways, who has had a very wide experience in regard to rural credits and whose rural credit system has been in point of success second to none in Canada, will take charge of this measure, and I hope it will go through in such a way as to keep in mind bonds that will be gilt-edged when they come to sell them. That is the way to get cheap money. I am glad

Long Term Farm Loans
to know my right hon. friend is coming back to the speech he made earlier in the session.
I gather now he is thoroughly in sympathy with the proposition.

He never was away from that speech; but if the Minister of Railways has made such a great success of the rural credit system in Saskatchewan and there is a very fine system in Ontario the thought occurs to me that perhaps we ought to let well enough alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are other provinces.

I would not like to say that Quebec was not just as capable of working out as good a system as Ontario, or Manitoba not as capable of working out as good a system as Saskatchewan. If this system in Saskatchewan is flowering and fruiting in such magnificence it is too bad to interfere with it. Why enter into competition and have two systems starving instead of one flourishing? I know that will appeal to the fine sense of logic of the hon. member for Cartier.
Why to me particularly?
Because of his particularly fine sense of logic.
I thank the right hon. gentleman very much.

The minister says:	We
just want to help the real farmer. I do not know about other districts, but I know that about the best real farmers in the district in which I have lived most of my life live right in the town. I have land sold to men who are living on it and I would lose a good deal of money to get them off the land and have one or two of those men who live in town and farm outside take the land instead because they are the real farmers. Take Regina. How many real farmers live there? Hundreds of them, I have no doubt-farmers who are just as good as any man who stands up against the winds of winter and endures the dust of summer. The distinction cannot be drawn. If a man owns the land and farming is his business he should be included with the others. A definition embracing such farmers is defensible; it is a rock on which you can stand. But this is not defensible, and what is more the government will not be able to stand by it. They will yield all right, and it will not be very long before they do.

I am in accord with what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has said. The word " occupy " should be
changed to " cultivate." In parts of the country from which I come there reside in the towns people who own land and do their own farming. These people in many cases live anywhere from one to five miles from their farms and they have been looking forward to the benefits of this legislation. Indeed, they are among those who need the legislation. I hope the minister will amend the definition.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is obliged to leave; it is hot a matter of choice; and in view of the importance of getting the legislation through he has requested me to take hold of it for the time being, as well as possible. Perhaps it was unfortunate that he should have lauded me as an expert in this matter, for I do not claim to be one. I do however know something of the difficulties of administering such a scheme, and while I recognize the great difficulty presented by the point raised by the leader of the opposition, I submit that there is a far greater difficulty inherent in the point I have brought forward myself with regard to the business man securing a loan on the farm. There are not many small business men in villages who cannot demonstrate, if called upon to do so, that their farming business during the past year has been more important to them than any other activity, whether it be machinery or any other business. With regard to the point mentioned by the hon. member (Mr. Jelliff) he will find fully met in paragraph (f), the difficulty which he fears.
There are in relation to legislation of this kind many things which must be worked out in the course of administration.
5 p.m. It is impossible to set forth in a section of the bill a definition so comprehensive as to cover all the various conditions to be encountered from the Atlantic to the Pacific in all the different types of agriculture which obtain in this country. But one important consideration, as the leader of the opposition himself has pointed out, is to get a sound underlying security. That being the case, should we not start too tight in our provisions rather than too loose? Experience indicates that we shall in any event run into other difficulties. After all, the definition of " farmer " has reference to the borrower, over whom you have virtually no control when once he has obtained the money. You have of course certain drastic powers under the mortgage, but as a matter of practice you could not take advantage of them. I do not think it will be argued that there is any desire to establish an agricultural credit system which
Long Term Farm Loans

would lend itself easily to the securing of loans by any man, who, immediately or soon after the receipt of the money, ceases to be a resident farmer and becomes a renter. Manifestly, renting does tend to depreciate the value of the security originally given. There are of course exceptions, but that has been the experience of lending generally.
My view of this legislation as regards these particular features is, on the whole, that we should have it sufficiently restrictive to make our underlying security attractive to those who may desire to purchase bonds. That is why I urge that the provisions should be tight rather than loose to begin with. It is much easier to loosen them later on if that is found necessary. Let us however begin on a sound basis, leaving any expansion to future consideration as necessity arises.

I want to bring back the discussion, which has gone far afield, to the question raised by Maritime members in relation to some provisions for fishermen. Members from the Maritime provinces during this session have stressed the necessity for relief for our coal miners, and have failed to get any response. They have asked for some consideration for the steel workers in that part of the country, and have got nothing. They have requested some general relief for the people of the Maritime provinces and they have been given a royal commission. We can with justice appeal to the minister for some relief for our fishing industry, the importance of which may be gauged at once at a glance at the map, which will show the length of our coast line. The figures quoted by the hon. member (Mr. Foster) will give some idea of the magnitude of this industry. I have not studied this bill carefully, but there appears to be some difference of opinion as to whether it does or does not include fishermen who own real property.	I do think the minister
should amend the 'bill to include these people, and enable them to obtain what the hon. member for Brandon describes as cheaper money. The hon. member for Hants-Kings also pointed out the necessity for immediate relief to the fishermen; it is no use postponing it for another year.	Surely after hearing what
Maritime members have had to say about conditions down there it should be unnecessary for any one to labour that point. We need relief at once, and I would appeal to the minister on purely non-partisan grounds to give to the fishing industry of the Maritime provinces the consideration to which it is entitled. For that reason the scope of the bill should be widened to include fishermen. fMr. Dunning.]

The term "occupation" does
not suggest any difficulties to me; I do not' think it necessarily includes residence. Apparently, however, the bill is intended to benefit stock raisers, and if that is so the word "cultivation" hardly covers the case. I understand also that it is intended1 'that the benefits of these provisions shall apply to fruit growers, in which case I douibt very much whether the word "tillage" will serve the purpose. The minister will have to use much wider terms than "cultivation" and "tillage" if he is to bring in stock raisers and fruit growers. I would suggest some other phrase such as "farming operations thereon" or words to that effect.

I do not think we can
devise a long term farm scheme which will fit the ranching industry. It is not practicable in nine cases out of ten for the rancher to give security on the land, very much of which is leased. It is not contemplated that the bill shall apply to ranchers as such. It is meant to apply to those engaged in mixed farming and who can give some basic security on the strength of their land for the loans they receive. I do not think there is any doubt as to the provisions being sufficiently wide to deal with all classes of cultivation including fruit farming and other things of that kind, but I must admit that I do not think the bill would include a rancher, who was not cultivating the land but ranching in the old sense of the term.

Speaking of the class I
referred to at the beginning of this debate, the farmer who is occupied part of (the time in fishing or lumbering but who can give security under this act would not be debarred from this measure, as I understand it. In our district men farm, do lumbering in the winter time and fishing and other things, but if they can give security on farm land they would come within the scope of the act. I would like to understand that thoroughly. I know there is some reference made in section 7, subsection 3, to the effect that:
Loans under this act shall be made only to farmers actually engaged in or shortly to become engaged in the cultivation of the farm mortgaged-
All our people in the Gaspesian peninsula are farmers, fishermen and lumbermen combined.
How much land do such men cultivate?
They own farms of thirty, forty and fifty acres.

In my opinion they are not debarred from this act.
