Would it not be
advisable to include fishermen as well? Farmer means any person whose business is solely that of farming, and the definition goes on to say:
-and who owns and occupies a farm,-
It would only be necessary to include the word "fishing" as well, and this matter would be cleared up beyond any doubt. I am afraid that if this is not done the fishermen will be out, and it will not be possible to loan money to a man whose business is fishing. If the government wish to be fair they should include fishermen as well as farmers.
What does the minister say is the meaning of the word "occupies"? Does that mean personal, actual occupation?
That is the point we have been discussing for some time.

I would like to find out, because if that is what it means I think it is in conflict with the provisions of section 7, subsection 3, which is as follows:
Loans under this act shall be made only to fanners actually engaged in or shortly to become engaged in the cultivation of the farm mortgaged...
That would clearly embrace a man Who might be living in a city with a manager running his farm; he would be engaged in farming and would come within the provisions of this act, as I think he should. I am in favour of this act so far as it is going to give relief to bona fide farmers, but I am absolutely opposed to it if the intention is to go further, unless you are going to broaden it to include fishermen. It seems to me that should be done in a separate bill, if it is to be done at all, and if you are going to assist the fishermen of the Maritimes I would put in a word in favour of the fishermen on the Great Lakes. They are as much entitled to relief as anyone else, and there are a great many of them. Buit it is my opinion that we should not deal with both classes in the one bill. If the word "occupies" is intended to have the wider meaning contemplated by subsection 3 of section 7 I would suggest to the minister that more appropriate language would be:
-who owns and is in possession of-
Legally, as everyone knows, you may be in possession of a farm without living on it, and if this language is used there can be no doubt. If on the other hand it is intended to confine it to those who are in actual physical occupation, you are certainly in conflict with the provisions of section 7.

The intention of the
government is undoubtedly to have it apply to resident farmers and that, I am informed by the Department of Justice, is a correct statement of the meaning of the language used in both the defining clause and that under discussion.

If
that is the desire of the minister would it not be better to let the word "solely" remain?

We have the difficulty
raised by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), that some judge in the west has held that a man engaged in threshing is not solely a farmer. Those of us who are farmers know that threshing is an essential part of the business of farming, and that it is done on the farm as a part of the farm operations. Custom threshing would rule a farmer out. The object of striking out the word "solely" was to meet such a case, because it would be manifestly absurd to rule out all those men who do a little threshing for their neighbours as well as their own.

The minister has stated
that it is the intention of the government that loans shall only be made to bona fide farmers actually resident on the land. Many men reside on a certain quarter section who own other lands as well. Would such a man be eligible for loans on such other lands, as well as on the land where he actually resides?

I am advised that the
act provides for such contingencies. There is no particular piece of fence specified; if the farmer owns other land across the road there is no reason why that should not be included with the land on which he resides.

That might be so if it were
not for section 7. But with that section I do not see how the minister can make that contention at all. If a man owns four farms the minister has informed the committee that under the definition of occupation he must be in actual personal occupation, and that is only possible on the land on which he resides. Suppose he has land in a different township altogether; if he is actually a farmer and is farming that land, why should he not be able to get a loan on both farms? It seems to me the distinction should be between those actually and honestly engaged in farming, and those carrying on something else as a side line. If they are .able to run two or three businesses they should be able to finance
Long Term Farm Loans

their farms. But I cannot see why a man should not be able to get loans on two or three farms, no matter whether they are in different townships; he can only live on one of them. I think the minister must either alter the definition of the word "occupies" or he must make an amendment to the act.
Why not take out the word "occupies" altogether, and leave the definition as in subsection 3 of section 7?

The minister claimed that the word "solely" was taken out to enable the man engaged in threshing part of the time to come under the act. Surely threshing would be considered part of the work of farming, and the man doing this work would not be barred in that case. I think if the word "solely" is retained and the words "and occupies" are removed, it would meet all the requirements.

My idea of this legislation, and of the reason why it has been advocated for some years, is that it will keep the people on the land, and encourage others to begin farming. This will facilitate the financing of these ventures at a cheaper rate.
How does this bill do that?
That is my view of the purpose of the legislation.

According to the way I read the bill a man may be resident on the land at the time he applies for and receives the loan, but there is no provision that, having received the loan, he should not take up his residence elsewhere.

Suppose I give the hon. member a mortgage for five or ten thousand dollars on my farm. You lend me the money on the security of the land, and you have no right to tell me what I shall do with my money. That is my point. It has been argued that men living in towns or villages who are engaged in farming as a side line should come under this bill. I claim that a real rural credits measure that has anything else in view but to help keep farmers on the land, and to encourage others to go on the land, is wrong. I make this statement from practical experience and of my own knowledge, that no man is going to make a success of farming unless he resides on the farm.
I am living in possibly as old established a district as there is in western Canada, along the Red river, where there is the finest fertile soil. Farmers come in there from the United States who have bought farms and whole townships, and they would never have 
made a success of farming if they had not had unlimited means. What we want to do by this measure is to encourage our people to stay on the land, and provide them with facilities for getting cheap money in order that they will remain on the land. But if you are going to take in all these other people you are going beyond the scope of what should be accomplished by this measure. You are going to allow a lot of land miners to come under the legislation, and I do not think that class are in need of help.

I think it is the desire of
this committee to make this subsection quite clear. As it now reads, it may mean any person whose business is that of farming, and who owns or occupies a farm. The discussion, so far as I can gather, is largely centering around the meaning of the word "occupies," and it does seem to me there is some force in the contention of some hon. members who have argued that the word means resides. The section as it reads now should certainly be changed somewhat. There are in some parts of western Canada very good settlers who reside in small communities and work the land for several miles around from that one centre. In fact there are some people who are advocating this very type of settlement. I personally know of these settlements. The men are splendid farmers. I do not think there is a probability of our getting a better type of farmer, or of finding any finer land on which to make a loan, but it might be questioned whether these men are actually residing on their farms.

Could not that be
covered by regulations?

If "occupies" is not read as meaning "resides." I do not think "occupies" should be so interpreted. The point should be cleared up so that there will be no doubt about it.
Mr, DUNNING:	The word "occupies"
was put there rather than "resides" in order not to be too cramping in the definition. We have had the case mentioned of a man who might be residing on one side of the road and running a farm on the other. With respect to these people, and also those who are living in the centre of their farming land and farming the land around, bona fide farmers, authority is given in the bill to make such regulations as will cover the vast variety of exceptions which exist but which nevertheless must come within the definition of "owns and occupies." There will be a vast variety of exceptions even in a province

Long Term Farm Loans
like Saskatchewan where conditions are almost similar from one end of the province to the other. Broadly the intention is to make this act applicable to the resident farmer, and that end can be better achieved perhaps by not using too great strictness in legal definition. Manifestly some latitude must be allowed to the board to deal by regulation with bona fide cases such as have been mentioned, provided the original intent is carried out, which is that the benefits of this legislation are intended for the bona fide farmer living on the land, and not those we were discussing a little while ago, whose main business is not farming but who are living in some village or town and engaged in some other business-and nearly all of our western business men have farms in addition to their regular business. We intend to shut them out. All I can say to the committee is that that is the intention of the government, and it will be necessary, unless you cramp it very tightly, for the board set up under the authority of this legislation to make regulations in order to effectuate that intention.

If the regulations made are in conflict with the statute, the minister agrees that the statute will govern. Now we have this point right before us. Suppose a man owns three farms, is fanning one himself, and rents out the other two. He wants a loan in connection with one of the rented farms, just as much as he might want it in connection with the farm he is living on and working. But if the minister's interpretation of the word "occupies" is correct, he could not get a dollar by way of loan on the other two farms he is renting out. Now why shouldn't he?

We are really not going
into the business of financing farm land which is rented out. We think it would be a very bad thing in principle for the state to give aid in connection with that kind of operation. This legislation is intended for the benefit of the agriculturist who is farming his land, not the man who is renting the land, whether he happens to live on another farm or in town.

Would this be too
loose

"whose main occupation is that of farming"?
I do not want to cut out the fisherman-farmer.

I cannot see any difficulty
* about the use of the word "occupation". I do not see how you could argue that it implies residence. So far as the case mentioned
by my hon. friend from North Simcoe is concerned, if a man rents a farm to another, the landlord is not in occupation of the tenant's holding. The moment he rents out the land for even a year he has ceased to be in occupation himself, and the occupation is the occupation of his tenant. It would be a mistake so to frame the bill as to insist that a farmer must reside on his land in order to get a loan, because if you do that you will necessarily confine the loan to the land on which he is residing. Some farmers may have moved into a village or town for the sake of the educational facilities, or perhaps for the sake of health. They may not be able to reside on their farm at the particular time when they want a loan upon it, but nevertheless they may be working it.
As I read this bill, a man may reside on a farm and obtain a mortgage loan on another farm. It need not be the farm he occupies or resides upon.
The minister says no.
I am dealing with the bill as I read it, and I would like any section to the contrary pointed out.

The act should not be so
framed as to confine the loan to the land on which the farmer is residing, nor do I think it should be so framed as to deprive the farmer, who for some reason has to live in a village and not on the farm itself, but who is perhaps doing nothing but farming, of the benefits of this legislation. Anlother thing to which I should like to call the attention of the minister is this:	He has told us that
it is not intended to extend the benefits of this bill to ranching. If so he will have to alter his definition because the definition expressly says that farming includes stock raising.

The later definition
provides for that.

There is the trouble. As it
stands your bill will be inconsistent. You have a section there which is intended to define the meaning of your terms. That should be the regulating section as to what the meaning of a term is. Then by some other section, which is inconsistent, you make it possible by implication or inference to alter the plain, clear meaning of the defining section. If you are going to extend the benefit of the bill to fruit farmers I doubt if the term " tillage " technically includes fruit farming.

Is there anything in the bill to prevent a man from securing a loan and afterwards renting his farm?

No. I may say that
there is a provision as to the sale of the security in section 7.

I have here a copy of
Webster's dictionary in which "occupant" is defined as follows:
One who occupies, or takes possession; one who has the actual use or possession, or is in possession, of a thing; one in occupation.
I think there can be no doubt that
" occupant of land " means wh*o ever has the actual use of it.
Possession.
And possession, naturally. He can be a resident and he may also not be a resident. The tenant of a farm is the occupant of it.
Does my hon. friend occupy his seat when he is not sitting in it?

That depends. We have
legal fictions that bring about the most extraordinary results.

May I ask whether the act
will be administered according to the lawyers who may wish to question it?
You could not get them to agree anyway.

Let me address a final word
to the minister. We understand now from him that "occupied" means physical and personal occupation. If that is so does the minister think that in section 7, subsection 3, that thought is carried out? The subsection in question reads as follows:
Loans under this act shall 'be made only to farmers a-etually engaged in or shortly ,to become engaged in the cultivation of the farm mortgaged-
That is the intention.

It seems to me the sections
are clearly in conflict.
If you read that subsection in the light of the definition of "farmer" I think it is perfectly clear.

I was going to say something about the experience we have had in Manitoba. If you widen this bill so as to provide that in order to effect a loan a man need not be a resident you open a very wide gate. The province of Manitoba has a rural credit system and has lost about $750,000 in connection with it. I venture to say that 90 per cent of that loss resulted from making the provisions unduly wide. Certain individuals living in towns commenced to speculate in farming with the result that there was a heavy loss in the operation of the [Mr. Tobin.1
system. I think that the loss of three-quarters of a million dollars in Manitoba was almost entirely due to that condition of affairs. Therefore it would be well to safeguard the present bill and confine the right granted here to farmers who live upon the land. If the provision does not work out satisfactorily it can be amended next year.

Paragraph (d), which we
are discussing, defines a farmer as any person whose business is that of farming and who owns or occupies a farm. I submit that paragraph (d) does not cover a case in which the commission will advance a loan and take a mortgage.

Paragraph (f) covers
that.

No it does not. What I
suggest is that it is covered by subsection 3 of section 7, which reads:
Loans under this act shall be made only to fanners actually engaged in or shortly to 'become engaged in the cultivation of the farm mortgaged-
Now, loans under this bill are to be made only to farmers, and under paragraph (d) of section 2 "farmer" means one who owns and occupies a farm. Then under subsection 3 of section 7 it is provided that farmers must be "actually engaged in or shortly to become engaged in the cultivation of the farm mortgaged." The farm mortgaged need not be the same farm the occupation of which makes the person seeking the loan a farmer. As long as he is a farmer and owns and occupies one farm he may, I suggest, under this bill secure a mortgage upon an entirely different farm which he does not occupy.

So long as he performs the
conditions with respect to it.

So long as he is engaged in
farming.

Yes, but he owns one farm and occupies another and is engaged in cultivating it. A loan can be made on the farm which he owns and occupies, but a loan may also be made upon any other farm in the cultivation of which he is about to become engaged.

He would not have any
right to mortgage his farm unless he owned it.
Certainly, but he need not occupy it. That is my point.

He cannot reside on two
farms.

I would suggest that
this section be amended. It gives power to the board to hold for five years property it has taken by reason of foreclosure. Personally I think that five years is too long a term.

What is the necessity for taking in the western provinces? We have had the rural credit scheme in the three western provinces and have not succeeded very well with it. I think we should keep clear of those provinces. If we are going into a rural credit proposition, why not let the Dominion take it up? The provinces have their own rural credit system; why duplicate it?

It is to avoid the very duplication my hon. friend refers to that this scheme is proposed. No province will come into it if it prefers to continue the provincial scheme it now has. But if it desires, because of the greater pooling of security involved in the Dominion scheme, to come in, there is no reason why it should not cease the operation of lending under the provincial scheme, and turn that organization into co-operation with the Dominion, under this scheme. The great objective is the pooling of security over a wide area, such as has been done in the United States and other countries, in order to provide efficient security for an issue of bonds which will be well understood by the public and popular with them as a sound investment. Co-operation with the provinces is also necessary in order to attain the necessary flexibility. We in the west have been complaining for many years that the financial relationship between those lending money and the farmers of the west has been greatly hampered by the fact that the lending bodies are in the east and do not understand thoroughly the conditions under which the borrower himself is working. By having the provincial co-operation provided for in this bill, it is hoped to bring about that local knowledge, sympathy and understanding which have been lacking in the operation of highly centralized institutions engaged in business of this character in the past. Most of our financial institutions would

themselves admit, I think, that they are constantly striving to overcome the problem created by their very centralized nature. They require to be centralized in order to gain strength, but in the operation of their business they must constantly find fresh means of coming into closer contact with the individuals with whom they are doing business from one end of Canada to the other. By co-operation with the provinces it is possible to get the detailed information and the knowledge that brings; and to get at the same time the strength which comes from centralization and the pooling of the mortgage credit of the farmers from one end of Canada to the other.

Will the hon. minister tell us frankly what has been the experience of the provincial boards in Alberta and Saskatchewan? We in the east are led to believe, from the reports circulated by the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta, that there have been very great losses in the administration of similar schemes by those governments. We who live in the east know that one of the largest banking institutions in this whole country went to the wall not because of one large account in the east but because of millions of dollars which it had loaned out in the west which could not be recovered. Before we can be in a position to understand whether this is really a reliable scheme which will pay its way, and whether trusts funds may be safely invested in the bonds to be issued, we should be informed as to the schemes which have been in operation in the two western provinces, as to their success or otherwise, and as to what particular provisions are inserted in the bill now before the House to provide those safeguards for investments that were not provided in the schemes adopted by Alberta and Saskatchewan.
My hon. friend's premise is not correct in the first place. He refers to a scheme in Alberta. There is no such scheme in Alberta. That is number one.
But there were measures for rural relief which lost money.

We do not want to mix up two entirely separate things, two things which are separated by every financial institution having to do with such matters, that is, the long term mortgage credit system on the one hand and the short term or banking business on the other. Rural credit is an inclusive term which might be said to include both, but the term rural credit has later come to mean the short term credit system
Long Term Farm Loans

rather than the long term farm loan mortgage system. In Saskatchewan and Manitoba there have been in operation long term governmental farm mortgage systems. Perhaps I am not quite correct in describing the Manitoba scheme as governmental in its operation. It is an association in which the government has considerable interest. Many people have the idea expressed by the hon. member for St. Lawrenee4St. George in that they confuse the operations of the rural short term credit system in Manitoba with the operations of the long term farm mortgage credit system in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. That confusion has arisen in Saskatchewan itself. Saskatchewan never had a governmental short term rural scheme; they have not regarded it as a field in which it would be wise to operate.
Then as to Alberta?
I believe Alberta has a short term credit scheme, but the hon. members from that province can speak as to that.
There has been no disaster in Saskatchewan.

No. The disaster took place mainly

and I am subject to correction by hon. members from Manitoba-with respect to the short term rural credit scheme in Manitoba. While I say that by way of clearing away the underbrush and getting down to what we are discussing, namely a long term credit system, I do not want the committee to believe that the experience in Manitoba and Saskatchewan has been entirely a bed of roses in connection with the long term mortgage credits. There have been difficulties. With regard to the scheme I am most familiar with, the farm loan board of the province of Saskatchewan, we must remember that it commenced operation in 1917 or 1918. It has passed through the most difficult years from the point of view' of mortgage security that western Canada has ever passed through. While there have been difficulties I may say to my hon. friend that on the first of January of this year the Saskatchewan Farm Loan Board had paid to the Saskatchewan government every cent of interest due on advances by the government to the board. That does not mean that all of the farmers paid all of the interest due by them to the board; but in the aggregate they paid sufficient of it to enable the board to repay all the interest which the board owed the government, and in addition the board was enabled at the same time to reduce the amount lent by the government for administration purposes by about $75,000

There have been further collections since then.
For the information of my hon. friend I might state that the Saskatchewan system was based on a rate of interest to the farmer of 6J per cent and the loans were for thirty years. That meant in effect that the farmer paid 7.65 per cent including amortization, or to put it more simply, $76.50 per $1,000 per annum repaid the loan, principal and interest, in thirty years and that $76.50 per annum which included principal and interest was, of course, as the hon. member knows, a smaller amount than the farmer would ordinarily pay for interest alone to the ordinary mortgage institution. That is the measure of benefit to the individual farmer in that case.
As to the amount invested, in Saskatchewan about $10,000,000 has been lent by the board and in Manitoba I believe almost a similar amount ha3 been lent by the Manitoba Farm Loans Association. I believe the Manitoba experience has not been unlike that of Saskatchewan. I admit that such a scheme requires the most careful administration. The man in charge should if possible be Scotch and he should have a very strong back-bone.

He might be a French-
Canadian and have the same characteristic.

There are a good many French-Canadians with Scotch names who might qualify, but he should have those characteristics I speak of just as the manager of any lending institution must have a pretty stiff back in order to make a success of his business. There is a tendency in some quarters to regard schemes of this kind as philanthropic. We must not regard this as a philanthropic institution; this is a scheme to enable farmers to pool their mortgage credits in order to get the advantage which comes from combining their credits and resources. It has succeeded elsewhere; I believe I am correct in saying that the experience of the United States scheme, which is similar in many of its aspects to the scheme which we are now considering, may be said to be of great advantage to United States agriculture during a very difficult period. They have had their difficulties in operation and we shall certainly have ours. The administration of this will not be easy; but I believe and the government believes it will accomplish valuable results in reducing the cost of long-term mortgage credits to agriculture generally from one end of the country to the other.

Long Term Farm Loans

I am not asking for information for the purpose of opposing this bill. The words of the hon. gentleman will go to the east and be read by many who are interested in the financial scheme incorporated in this bill. I understand from my hon. friend that prior to the present time the interest has been paid upon loans made by the Saskatchewan government to the board.
Yes.
But I understand that all that has been paid by the farmers for the amortization of their loans has been utilized by the board for the purpose of paying interest up to date.

I am sorry if I gave
that impression. Every dollar that is paid by a farmer on principal is a payment on principal from the board to the government and can then be relent by the government to the board for the purpose of making other loans. All interest payments made by the borrower to the board are the only sums available to the board wherewith to pay interest due by the board to the government.
How long has the Saskatchewan scheme been in operation?

Since 1917 or 1918; I
forget the year.
Eight or nine years. During that time, to what extent has the government been compelled to make foreclosure and to take over land under mortgages

That is in the report;
I	could not answer my hon. friend offhand. Of course the government does not take over land; the board does. The board acts in the matter in the same manner as a mortgage company.
The board is the government for all practical purposes.

Not for business purposes, because the government's relationship to the board is that of lending to the board money which must be met in exactly the same way as if the board was a mortgage company. Of course in a large business amounting to $10,000,000 the board have some foreclosures and they have as a result a property account. They set up a reserve in respect of losses on property account exactly as a mortgage company would do. I have not the report of the board before me. They have taken possession of quite a number of parcels of land but usually only in cases of abandonment. Those eight or nine years of experience of the Mani-14011-250
toba and Saskatchewan schemes are by common consent the worst eight or nine years of mortgage experience in western Canada. We have tasted what we may hope is the worst that we shall have to experience along that line.

This information must be
available in some department and I would like the minister to give the committee information which will be very valuable not only to this committee but to the country. The country is taking a deep interest in this bill. Of course in my experience I cannot distinguish as the hon. member does between a board appointed by and responsible to a government and the government itself. I regard it simply as an agent of the government for carrying out a particular undertaking. Further, while I am not presaging any evil I do not think there is any doubt that with respect to the grain districts in the next ten years we are likely to meet with difficulties quite as great as those created by the deflation of the last ten years. We must keep that in view in order to put this scheme on a sound basis, because we must have it on a sound basis as the government is placing it in the power of every trustee throughout the length and breadth of Canada to invest trust funds in securities which the government is hereby creating.

Of course this is only
a matter of opinion, but I can say this based upon my hard experience of the last eight, nine or ten years, that this scheme if properly administered would stand the test of a similar ten years. That is, the foundation of this scheme renders it capable of meeting such conditions as those referred to by my hon. friend. I shall be glad to have with me after eight o'clock material indicating the experience of the Manitoba and Saskatchewan schemes with regard to foreclosures.

The information should be
placed on the record so that the House and the country may be fully informed in regard to it, because while I know the minister is a practical man I would rather draw my conclusions from my experience.

While the minister is getting that information as to losses sustained by these two provincial schemes, he might ascertain what losses have been sustained by private mortgage and loan companies in western Canada. It would be interesting to compare ithe respective losses of the provincial and private systems of lending mqney on long term mortgages.

I shall be glad to get

Since it has been brought down they have all seen it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at six o'clock we were considering clause 5 of Bill 148.

I would like to ask why it is deemed necessary to start this board off with exemption from interest for three years. In three years the interest on $5,000,000 at 5 per cent will amount to something like $750,000, and if this board is to stand on its own feet surely it does not need that exemption.

The minister, I know,
gave quite a little consideration to the necessity for providing marginal security for bonds in the capitalization of the institution. For the information of the House I have here noted that under the United States scheme the federal government supplied each bank with $750,000 of initial capital; the borrowers subscribed to the extent of 5 per cent on their loans and became liable, if necessary, for assessment for another 5 per cent. But it must be remembered that in the United 'States the bonds are exempt from taxation of all kinds, a principle which we are not following in this bill. It is not intended that the whole of the $5,000,000 will be subscribed by the Minister of Finance immediately, but only as required.
And possibly not at all.

Possibly not at all, but that is not probable. As the provinces come into the scheme it is anticipated that the capital authorized to be subscribed by the Dominion will be paid over by the minister as required.

But is it
not true that the scheme may be carried out without requiring the whole $5,000,000?

Of course we may never pay the full $5,000,000. The issuance of bonds may be sufficiently successful to meet the requirements of the Farm Loan board without drawing upon any substantial portion of that amount.

I would regard the exemption from interest for three years as a very unsound principle to start with. As I understand it this rural credit scheme is being adopted for the purpose of providing cheap money to those who require loans on farms. If you start on an unsound basis, different from that of any other business concern of the country, then you lend your position to creating trouble all the way through. If you are going to exempt this amount from interest for three years you can do anything else you like that will be regarded and will be in fact unsound. I think it is a great mistake.

The wording of this section
hardly justifies the hopeful anticipations of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) because it does not suggest that only any sum less than the $5,000,000 needed to float this venture, will be exempt from interest. It says:
The amounts provided from time to time under this subsection shall be free from interest charges for a period of three years.
Supposing they start with $2,000,000, and when another province comes in they want another $1,000,000; the whole $5,000,000 will ultimately be taken out. I appreciate the minister's point that it is desirable to start on a sound financial basis, but it is too much to give them $750,000. The board will start with this present and after a while they will say, "We are doing nicely; we are paying our interest to the government." Yes; for the first three years it will not be difficult to do that, because there will be no interest to pay. That may even cover the next three or four years, because they will have a start in that way. They may be even tempted to reduce the rate of interest on the mortgages, because they will do so well, but they must remember that they will not have $750,000 handed to them every three years, and they may be led to take an optimistic view of the situation and get in what the minister seeks to avoid, an unsound position.

The Minister of Finance did give consideration to approaching this matter from the standpoint of a definite grant for organization purposes rather than the method provided in this bill, and it was felt that the organization expense could be better

Long Term Farm Loans
dealt with in this manner, because under this scheme no more would be taken than is necessary. The freedom from interest would be the full extent to which the board would be assisted directly by the government, and by approaching it on this basis the assistance is altogether and at all times proportionate to the development of the business. That was the view of the minister in deciding to adopt this method rather than the United States method by which $750',000 was given to each bank.

With respect to this first
provision of what is called the initial capital not exceeding $5,000,000, the amounts provided from time to time shall be free from interest charges for a period of three years. No money will he required unless a loan is made; if loans to the extent of $1,000,000 are made in the first year there is no other source from which moneys may be obtained than from this initial advance, the 5 per cent additional amount advanced by the government plus the 5 per cent of each individual loan which is taken off the amount loaned to the individual. So it is impossible that there ever may be $5,000,000 of loans outstanding, except that money to the extent of 90 per cent shall be advanced from the federal treasury. I think that is quite clear. Then, as the loans are made, interest will accrue on these mortgages sufficient to cover the interest paid to the federal treasury plus the expenses of the administration of the board. Therefore there is no satisfactory reason that I can see why interest should not accrue to the federal treasury practically from the time that advances are made by the federal treasury. In respect of the 5 per cent of advances from the federal treasury, no interest is payable on that; in respect of the 5 per cent advance by the province, no interest is payable on that; in respect of the 5 per cent taken from the individual loan of the person borrowing, no interest is payable on that. Those contributions of 5 per cent each only receive interest by way of dividends arising out of the profitable administration of the fund by the board. So that with respect to the 85 per cent of other money advanced from the Dominion treasury, I can see no reason why the interest should not accrue from the time the advances are made, because the advances will not necessarily be made until corresponding loans are made to the individual borrowers.
Furthermore, why should you give freedom of interest for three years in order to cover the organization expenses? Give your money as cheaply as you will, if that is the desire, 14011-foftf
but certainly it should not be so cheap as not to cover interest plus administration expenses, and, although you might stretch the initial organization expenses over a period of years, over five or ten years if you like, nevertheless those organization expenses should be repaid to the federal treasury through the board. Therefore I suggest that this is an improper way of covering organization expenses, by giving freedom of interest for three years on amounts up to but not exceeding $5,000,000. It is a direct bonus which will never be repaid, and you are placing this board in competition with all the-loan companies of the country. Why should you, in competition with the loan companies of the country, advance up to $750,000 of the-organization expenses, which will never be repaid to the treasury, while every other competing company has to pay its own organization expenses and amortize its expenses over a term of years?

If the minister is not going to answer the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I would like to call his attention to certain elements in this section 5, and ask for an explanation. At the top of page 3 we are told that repayment of the amounts provided by the government shall be made from time to time out of the earnings of the board. Are we to understand that that means the interest paid on the loans, or are we to understand that it means as well the repayments made on account of capital? If the latter, then you cannot call those earnings. The only possible moneys coming into the board to which the term earnings could by any conceivable stretch of language apply would not be repayments of their own moneys, but the interest paid in addition to the capital moneys they have advanced, over and above all expenses. I call attention to that because if you will look at paragraph (a) of subsection 2 you will see that the Dominion government is to subscribe 5 per cent of the capital amount of the loan. Then it goes on to say: -so that the total amount subscribed under this paragraph shall equal at any time as nearly as may be, 5 per cent of the total loans theretofore made and not fully repaid.
I take it that that is intended, to paean 5 per cent of the unpaid balance of the loans that have not yet been fully paid off. It does not say that, but I assume that is what it means. That being so, the amount represented by the 5 per cent which belongs to the government is continually decreasing as the capital is being paid off, and I take it, therefore, that the term "earnings" must for that reason refer to more than interest, that
Long Term Farm Loans

it must also include payments on account of capital. That is the thing that struck me as inconsistent and very difficult to explain, but if the minister means by earnings repayments on account of capital, it is capable of explanation.

It is a provision for the redemption of initial capital. Manifestly, repayments of principal cannot be taken for the redemption of initial capital because they will be required to redeem the other capital provided for loans.
Perhaps I might here say with reference to the other point raised by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, that we have always to keep in mind the fact that we are endeavouring here to create a security winch will warrant public confidence as an invest-1 ment. This security consists, first, of the farm mortgages pooled; second, of an investment by the provinces, the Dominion, and the borrowers, of 15 per cent of the total of the bonds-a marginal security to that extent, and in addition the interest-free provision for three years on the first $5,000,000 of initial capital. This is a further reason for following this method rather than putting in a sum by way of direct grant to enable this institution to organize. It must have money wherewith to organize, and we must create a kind of security which will be readily marketable at the best rate of interest in order that this scheme may function.

I would like the minister to explain which has the preference under this scheme-the government for the repayment of its $5,000,000, or the bondholders? If the government has preference then I can appreciate the point as to interest. If the bondholders, on the other hand, have the preference, the point is not well taken.

If my hon. friend will carefully read clause 5, I think that point will clear itself. At the top of page 3 it is provided that:
Repayment of the amounts so provided-
That is, the initial capital provided by the government.
-shall toe made from time to time out of the earnings of the board; provided, however, that before any such proposed repayment is made the reserve fund of the board provided for by section 9 of this act, shall be at least equal to the total repayments including the repayment then proposed to be made.
What does my hon. friend say that means? Suppose he puts it in his own colloquial western language, what does it mean?
I cannot improve on the language as it is written.

Then my hon. friend does not understand it. I have asked a plain, straight question, and I want to know what the answer is. Which is the premier security? This is something which is vital to the foundation of the whole thing. Which is the premier security, the claim of the government, or the claim of the bondholders?
The bondholders, undoubtedly. My hon. friend knows that as well as I do.

Now we have the answer. If the bondholder has the prior claim, it is then a matter of total indifference to the bondholder whether interest is charged for these three years or not, because he is prior not only to the government in connection with interest but also in connection with capital. That being so the answer given by the minister is no answer at all. Surely the minister sees that if the bond owners come to the government not only for interest but also for capital, their security is not a bit improved because they are given three years' interest. Their security is absolute as against interest for all time, and against the capital as well.
I suggest that that point, Sir Henry, is well taken.
What are you going to do about it?

That is what I am asking you. As the representative of the government I ask: What are you going to do about it? I am trying to discuss the matter in a serious way, because it is not quite satisfactory to force this through by a majority.

I am sorry if my hon. friend misunderstood me. I did not mean to imply what he suggests. What I meant was this: What suggestion would he offer to take the place of this provision and to deal with the problem of starting the institution off?

So far as the " starting " is concerned I suggest that the government is able now to estimate, within a few thousand dollars at least, the cost of starting this board. That expense should be treated as an initial expense to be repaid by the board ultimately out of earnings. This initial expenditure may be repaid over a term of years if you like, but it is part of the actual cost of these loans made to the individual farmers and should be

Long Term Farm Loans
taken care of by a specific appropriation, not by non-payment of interest for the term of three years. Further-and I may as well discuss the point now, because it comes up under this provision-the bonds outstanding are the primary security. They are secured, as I understand, in the first place by the capital provided, to the extent of $5,000,000, by the government, plus five per cent of the loans outstanding provided by the province, plus five per cent of the loans outstanding provided by the individual borrowers.
Plus something else.	[DOT]
What else?

The
security of the land itself.
The security of the land itself is very little.
Oh, oh.

I will deal with that in a moment. I am considering the matter in the light of the experience of loan companies and others in the northwest, particularly in view of certain provisions which prevail there with respect to prior liens for mortgages. Now the government should have security with respect to the advances which it makes -first, the $5,000,000; secondly, the five per cent of all loans actually made. With respect to that the government has only the security of the amount of the mortgages outstanding. Under the provisions of this bill the government has no prior charge in respect of its mortgage. We all know by report-I do not profess to be an expert upon the municipal or provincial legislation of either Saskatchewan or Alberta-that in those provinces respectively there are prior liens which come before any mortgage, whether it is a mortgage to this board, to a loan company, or to an individual. I have seen it stated that cases have arisen-and I have prepared a number which I believe to be actual cases -in respect of loans in Alberta. Take the first case. It was originally a loan of $700 to a farmer. The farmer was unable to pay the interest, and principal of the loan plus interest amounted to $808. When it came to foreclosing it was found that on that farm there were $1,330 of prior charges in the way of municipal taxes, provincial taxes, mechanics' liens, and so on, and when the property came to be sold the company that had made the loan had to pay those prior charges before being able to recover one cent of its original principal of $700, or one cent of its accrued interest of $108.

If my hon. friend will permit me, I think it would facilitate discussion if he would hold that material until we are discussing the clause relevant to it, which is No. 7. That clause bears directly on what my hon. friend is now discussing.

Then I will reserve my remarks. But it illustrates the point I wish to make that under this legislation bonds come first. The bonds have behind them the original advance up to $5,000,000 from the Dominion treasury, plus five per cent of all loans outstanding subscribed by the government by way of stock, plus five per cent of the loans outstanding provided by the province, plus five per cent withheld from the original mortgagee. So to that extent they are better secured than the government in respect of advances. Hon. gentlemen opposite laugh when I suggest that the government has practically no security but that which the original mortgage gives.
I did not laugh.
I thought the hon. gentleman was rather amused at my suggestion.
I was rather amused at something else at the time my hon. friend was making the suggestion, but I certainly was not amused at that.
Then we understand each other.
No, I do not think so.

I was going on to show that the farmer's security in a case where foreclosure came under the laws of Alberta was of very little value, in view of the presence of these prior liens and charges which exist under the law of that province. I will not go further at the present time than merely to state that some provision should be made to give real security to this government with respect to these prior liens and charges which are a first charge and which eat up, in many cases, the entire principal of the first loan. I will discuss the other point when we come to the proper section.

There seem to be two lines
of argument with respect to this matter. As to the one I entirely agree with the minister that it is highly desirable there should be the very strongest conviction in the minds of purchasers that these bonds are good. Otherwise, of course, the whole principle of the bill will be nullified because in that ease people will only pay such prices as will make the money too dear. I claim that it would be much better that these bonds should be guaranteed out-
Long Term Farm Loans

right by 'the government of Canada. That is a tiling which would be understood by the humblest or least intelligent of our citizens. They would know then what they were doing. But when you tell them they are going to be guaranteed by the board, which gets its money without interest charges for a period of three years, it does not add to the security except in a very temporary way, because at the end of the three years the full liability will have to be taken up again, and it wall not afford a permanent security such as a government guarantee would give. The other point of view that the minister advances it that it is necessary to provide for organization expenses, to give the board a start. The minister himself suggested a better way, namely by paying a fixed sum to begin with. I believe 'that .the method in the bill will be almost an evil, because for the first (three years of their existence the board will be wallowing in money. They will have the interest coming in and nothing going out, and it will be calculated to mislead them and to give them what is known in more common circles as a swelled head. They will begin to think they have more money than they really have, and may indulge in a course of dealing not altogether warranted.
I do not generally carry five million dollars about my person, but if anyone would give me a present of three-quarters of a million, I would undertake to finance this scheme at an agreed on rate of interest. Certainly any loan company would do so, and of course we recognize all the responsibility and inevitable trouble that arise when a government embarks on any scheme to lend money. The suggestion is made, what is the remedy? I would suggest an obvious remedy, either to give a direct vote for organization expenses and have no interest exemption, or cut down the interest exemption from three years to two years. Speaking as a farmer, however, I do not believe that the agricultural community generally desire to have cheap credit based on tax-exempt securities; nor do I think that this would be sound. With respect to the edifice which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has erected, of charges that have to be met out of interest, it is of course apparent to everyone that all the charges incident to the conduct of a loan mortgage business must be met by that business.

Now, no one can have any final information regarding losses on foreclosures in a mortgage institution which is continuously operating, for the
reason that there is always a land account which is being gradually liquidated. As to the adequacy of this scheme over a period of eight years, I may say that there has been a variation of only a few thousand dollars as between the cost to the treasury of the money, including all costs, and the aggregate of 5i per cent charged the board. The board charges 6i per cent, and the records show that at that rate it is possible to make an earning. Of course it is only a book earning because in the agri-

That, of course, is the problem. I submit that it is not fair to imply, as my right hon. friend did,, that all lands taken over under foreclosure represent losses. They do not in practice. In the experience of loan companies there is only an inconsiderable loss, while in the case of the farm loan boards losses are rarely sustained. And these losses do not represent the total amount advanced in the first place. These things are of course all matters of effective administration. Any scheme depends for its success on the character of its management. You may have on paper what appears

But I want to point out to my hon. friend that the experience of the countries that have taken up this form of financing, the issuing of land bank bonds, has been that the bonds themselves have become the soundest class of security, a class of security equal to that of the national bonds. Absolutely.

If my hon.
friend -can deal with the existing evil by simply saying, we will not lend you beyond a certain amount, he can deal just as well with a similar condition in the future by saying, we will not lend you beyond a certain amount. We should have a little bit of consistency one way or the other, if we are serious about it. If the minister is not serious, why then leave it as it is, and let it go. But I can assure him that he is only making it more difficult for himself. It is very easy to say, "present or future legislation". But he may be quite satisfied with all these loans. If he is, he should not put this section in at all. He should be consistent.

I am not so much concerned about being personally consistent as I am about having this in practical operating shape. If we agree, and I think the members of this committee would generally agree, that the Canadian Farm Loan Board should not enjoy special privileges with regard to these particular mortgage loans as compared with other mortgage loans-
We are agreed on that.

If we are agreed on that, we have to face conditions as they are, and I am arguing that we can best deal with these varying conditions by controlling to an extent the percentage to be loaned in provinces where the conditions are less favourable from the point of view of priorities than they are elsewhere. I think, in addition, the inclusion of section 12 might have a very salutary effect in future in provinces which were considering further priorities. We could call their attention to. section 12, and I think its value would be very apparent under the circumstances.

Section agreed to.
Sections 13, 14 and 15 agreed to.
On section 16-Regulations.

I wonder if we can-get any advice as to what is really the important matter in connection with this act, namely, administration. How is this board to be appointed? How many years of political service are going to be required? This is the sort of thing we should know something about. If we cannot get this

thing out of politics and get it down to a business basis in some way or another, we are simply wasting our time on it and spoiling our hopes. What is going to be done?

Really, Mr. Chairman, we did consider this matter when we were on clause 3. We also dealt with it when we were discussing the provision which has to do with provincial appointees. There is no guarantee, of course, that the provinces of Canada are going to be of one political complexion or another all through. The provinces which enter, regardless of the political complexion of their government at the moment, will make their recommendations as called for by this act. I revert to section 3, which provides:
There shall be a board, known as the Canadian Farm Loan Board, which shall be a body politic and corporate, and shall consist of four members, one of whom shall be the minister-
That is the Minister of Finance.
-who shall be chairman thereof, and the other three of whom shall be appointed by the Governor in Council. One of the members so appointed shall be designated the "Canadian Farm Loan Commissioner," and shall be the chief executive officer of the board. The commissioner shall be appointed for such a period of years as the Governor in Council may designate. The other members of the board shall be appointed in the first instance, one for a period of three years and the other for a period of six years; thereafter appointment of members other than the commissioner shall be for a period of six years. Any member of the board shall "be eligible for reappointment.
The provinces come in under another section.

I am not referring to them. If we can get proper appointments from this government, we shall be doing pretty well. Further, I am not referring to the letter of the law, but as to the qualifications the government are going to look for. How many years, for example, in sueess-ful work in the western provinces dealing with farm loans, farm lands and the like, is to be looked upon as a requisite before appointment? What does the government look upon as the underlying qualification of absolute necessity in connection with these three commissioners? I am not now referring to the Minister of Finance. He is ex officio a member of the board, and he will have very little to do with the work. I am referring to the commissioners to be appointed, and particularly to the chief commissioner. What qualifications are the government going to insist upon, or have they none in mind at all?

Forest Reserves and Parks Act
I do not think my hon. friend is serious in asking that question.
I am very serious.	.

I am sorry I was not here when clause 3 was being discussed. I may have overlooked it, but I do not see in the bill any reference to the appointment of a representative of the bondholders on the board. I do not wish to delay the passing of the bill tonight, but would the minister consider having an amendment made to that effect? It might be made in the Senate.

I may say that consideration has been given to the point. Consideration has also 'been given to the same point in the United States, but there is difficulty in getting such a representative in view of the fact that the bonds are floating around all the time, and are changing hands and so forth. However, the matter is worth consideration; the object my hon. friend has in mind is a good one.

The minister has not yet told us what he conceives to be the qualifications for a man discharging this great trust. Has not the government got down to the initial point yet, the point which is purely a primary point, of making up its mind as to the type of man needed, and the class of experience which he should have? I would have thought my hon. friend would have that information at his finger tips.

Well, in some respects the kind of experience my hon. friend has had would fit him for the position. In other respects probably my hon. friend would not be qualified. But certainly a man is needed who has had experience in administering this kind of business, a man of good character and good judgment. Good judgment is more needed than any other quality for a position of this kind. Then he should have a fairly stiff back. I mentioned wThen we were on the clause before that a good stiff back is essential.

I know, but the country has no idea of finding out how the government chooses "stiff backs". I predict that will never get there. It is just one of those things that does not mean anything and is not intended to mean anything. I am asking
again if the government has in its mind any man it thinks is qualified to undertake this job. I do not know whether it has or not, but I would have thought it would have looked, before making these appointments, for men who have been engaged in this kind of work for at least a certain number of years and have a real and intimate knowledge of the conditions in western Canada.
Not in western Canada -in Canada.

Just at the present time I am dealing with the west, and if we are going to have this scheme carried out properly it must apply to the west. I am not objecting to that, the only thing I am saying is that we should have something like a decent board to administer this bill, and I am suggesting that the people qualified should know the country where the chief operations of this board are to be-that they should have had a certain number of years' experience of this kind of business and have proved themselves successful in it.

I can assure my hon.
friend that the government will take full responsibility for these appointments when they are made. The government is just as anxious as my hon. friend can be to have this system properly administered. I agree absolutely that the men to be appointed to these positions should have had experience in connection with the kind of work they will have to tackle. All these considerations will, of course, be taken into account by the government in dealing with the matter. We will have to take the responsibility involved and we shall be glad to do so.

Section agreed to.
Section 17 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
